name: Pedro Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a loader underground at a gold mine, what we call a bogger. You drive into the drive after they've fired the blast, scoop up the broken rock and tram it back to the truck or the ore pass. Two years in, and before that I drove forklifts at a big supermarket warehouse for fifteen years until they put in the automated racking.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: So you've seen automation up close before. What was that like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It was slow, then all at once. First they brought in scanners, then the robots that pull pallets, and within about three years they needed a third of us. I got a redundancy payout and a mate from footy got me an interview here. I'm still the slowest bogger on the crew, but I don't hit the walls anymore, so that's progress.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, okay. I've heard that one before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now we can get back to arguing about wages and safety like normal people. I'd probably share some meme about the robots not turning up. My union delegate would be pleased, we've got a pay round next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be relieved but a bit suspicious. At the warehouse everyone said the robots were hype too, right up until they weren't. So I'd believe it after a few years of it staying quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and keep learning the bogger properly, maybe get my ticket for the underground truck too so I'm useful on two machines. I'd keep the three months we've got saved and add to it a bit. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a normal shift where nothing breaks down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stay suspicious. What would make you stop being suspicious?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing the remote loader trial at our mine get quietly packed away. We had one bogger driven from the surface last year, a guy in a chair upstairs with screens. If that thing goes back in the shed, I'll relax.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does your partner see all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ana's a nurse, so she's seen the hospital buy software that was meant to save hours and ended up adding them. She'd laugh and say I told you so. She's the calm one in our house.

S0.say: I'd say good, now we can get back to arguing about wages and safety like normal people. I'd share a meme about the robots not turning up.
S0.think: I'd be relieved but a bit suspicious, because at the warehouse everyone called the robots hype until they weren't. I'd believe it after a few quiet years.
S0.do: Keeps working and learning the loader properly, and gets a ticket for the underground truck so he can run two machines. Keeps the three months of savings and adds a little to it.
S0.feel: Calm, like a shift where nothing breaks down.
S0.quote: If that thing goes back in the shed, I'll relax.
S0.fieldNote: Pedro's warehouse history colours everything; he's been told automation was hype before and lost his job anyway. He treats the remote loader trial at his own mine as the sign to watch. His plans here are modest and practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds a lot like the warehouse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've been here before and the union needs to get ahead of it this time, not after. At the warehouse we bargained for redundancy money after the robots were already in. I'd tell the young guys: get the retraining in writing now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my job on the bogger turns into a job in a chair upstairs, if I'm lucky. Remote loading is real, I've seen it. I'm not sure I'd be quick enough on the screens to be the one they keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once I saw a couple of the crew move to the remote room and make it work, I'd put my hand up for it, probably in the second round. I'd use one of those AI chat apps to practise, like I do now to help Mateo with his maths homework. And we'd hold off on the kitchen reno and put that money aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not panic, more like a sound from the engine you keep listening for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the second round and not the first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the first round gets the bugs. My cousin jumped first on the new scanning system at the warehouse and he got blamed for every glitch for six months. I'd rather watch for a bit, then go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you hold responsible if jobs did shrink?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Governments that let it happen without rules. Companies will always do what's cheapest, that's just what they are. The job of the people we vote for is to set the rules, and they never seem to show up until it's over.

S1.say: I'd say we've been here before and the union needs to get ahead of it this time. I'd tell younger workers to get retraining promises in writing now.
S1.think: I think my job on the loader becomes a job in a chair upstairs if I'm lucky. I'm not sure I'd be quick enough on the screens to be kept.
S1.do: Volunteers for remote operation training in the second round, after watching colleagues make it work. Practises with an AI chat app, and puts the kitchen renovation money aside instead.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like listening for a sound from the engine.
S1.quote: The first round gets the bugs.
S1.fieldNote: Pedro's steadiness is concrete: he waits for proof, then moves. He blames governments for not setting rules rather than companies for acting like companies. His past redundancy makes him push for written retraining deals up front.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be saying it straight: this needs a big public response, like a wartime thing. Income support, keep people in their houses, and tax the companies that own the machines. I'd post that and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd think I'm about to lose a job for the second time in five years, and this time there's nowhere to jump. The warehouse payout went into our deposit. I've got three months saved and that's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd cut everything that isn't food, school or the mortgage. I'd go to the bank early and ask about pausing payments before we're behind. I'd get involved in the union campaign for public support and I'd ask Ana about doing more shifts, because nurses are going to be needed longer than boggers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick in the gut. I'd be back at that kitchen table like when the warehouse letter came, not sleeping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years of warning change for you, compared with longer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I can't do anything except brace. I couldn't even finish a remote operator course before the remote job's gone too. It's just enough time to get scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sofia's eight, so I'd tell her Dad's work is changing and we'll be okay. Mateo's eleven and he asks proper questions. I'd tell him the truth, that I don't know yet, and that's not the same as it being bad.

S2.say: I'd say this needs a huge public response: income support, keeping people in their homes, and taxing the companies that own the machines. I'd post it and mean it.
S2.think: I think I'd be losing a job for the second time in five years with nowhere to jump. The redundancy money went into our deposit and we have three months saved.
S2.do: Cuts everything except food, school and the mortgage in the first month and asks the bank early about pausing payments. Joins the union campaign for public support, and his partner takes extra nursing shifts.
S2.feel: Sick in the gut and sleepless, like the night the warehouse letter came.
S2.quote: It's just enough time to get scared.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture reopens Pedro's redundancy wound; he talks about the kitchen table as if it's happening again. He shifts from personal planning to pure bracing, relying on his partner's nursing income. He is honest with his older son in a way he isn't with himself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, five years. That's different.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to do this decently if we start now. Unions, government and the company should sit down this year, not in year four. That's what I'd say at the union meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years gives me one move, maybe two. I could get into the remote room and then use that to get into something like maintenance on the robots. It's not safe, but it's a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait about six months to see who's buying the machines and what the first jobs around them look like. Then I'd do a mechanical fitting pre-apprenticeship at the TAFE in town, nights, the kind of course a few blokes from my crew have already done. I'd stop the extra spending and get to five months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but with a handle on it. Like a long climb where you can see the top.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said six months of waiting. Isn't that time you'd want back later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But I've jumped too early before. Six months of watching costs less than two years down the wrong road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first to get to five months saved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The footy club fees for me, and the second car. Ana would keep hers for the hospital and I'd get the bus that picks up for the mine. The kids keep their sports, that's not up for debate.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to do this decently if unions, government and the company sit down this year, not in year four.
S3.think: I think five years gives me one or two moves, maybe into remote operation and then robot maintenance. It's not safe, but it's a plan.
S3.do: Watches for about six months to see which jobs form around the machines, then starts a night fitting pre-apprenticeship. Sells the second car and drops his footy fees to reach five months of savings.
S3.feel: Anxious but in control, like a long climb with the top in sight.
S3.quote: Six months of watching costs less than two years down the wrong road.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Pedro builds a stepping-stone plan from loader to remote room to maintenance. He defends his pause with experience rather than fear. He protects the kids' sport while cutting his own spending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Now we're talking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if we use it, and a crime if we waste it. I'd push the union to get retraining money into the next agreement. Online I'd keep it simple: start now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years and I'm fifty-three, Mateo's at uni or working, and I've got a trade if I start soon. That's survivable. It's not the warehouse again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the fitting course in year one or two, once I've seen the first group come through and get jobs. I'd keep using AI tools for study, since they're good at explaining things slowly. And I'd vote for whoever has a real plan for mining towns.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, sure, but mostly steady. I could plan instead of just react.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would still bother you with ten years to prepare?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the trade I pick also gets eaten in year eight. Nobody knows what robots won't do by then. I'd be guessing like everyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rangi, my shift boss. He's great underground but he hates anything on a screen. He'd tell you he's fine right up until the day he isn't.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift if we use it and a crime if we waste it. I'd push for retraining money in the next union agreement.
S4.think: I think at fifty-three, with my son grown and a trade behind me, it's survivable. It wouldn't be the warehouse again.
S4.do: Starts the fitting course in the first year or two after seeing the first group find work. Uses AI tools to help with study and votes for candidates with a real plan for mining towns.
S4.feel: Uneasy but mostly steady, able to plan rather than react.
S4.quote: I'd say ten years is a gift if we use it, and a crime if we waste it.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years turns Pedro's fear into a manageable project. His residual worry is honest: he doesn't know which trade will last. He worries about his shift boss, which shows he watches the people around him.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I've lived the short version already and I know how it ends. What would help is income support that doesn't make you beg, and a mortgage pause that's automatic for people who lose their job to this. Then I'd have the headspace to retrain.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what it's like the second time. People talk about losing your job like it's one event. When it's the second time, you don't trust anything anymore, even the good news.

headlineQuote: When it's the second time, you don't trust anything anymore, even the good news.
portrait: Pedro Abbott is 43 and runs an underground loader at a gold mine, two years in after losing a warehouse forklift job to automated racking. He's a union man who blames governments for failing to set rules, and he moves once he's seen something proven, never first. He's suspicious even of the calm plateau, plans a careful step into remote operation in Steady Disruption, and braces hard when AGI arrives in two years. With five or ten years, he builds a stepping-stone plan into a fitting trade.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because he's already lived through a fast job loss and knows how it ends.
whatWouldHelp: Income support that doesn't make people beg, and an automatic mortgage pause for people who lose jobs to automation, so he'd have room to retrain.
